Empirical Research Plan: do India’s flagship environmental regulations improve pollution and infant health?  

==================================================================

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------  
Method: Staggered-adoption Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented with event-study dynamics.  

Why appropriate?  
• Three national programmes were rolled out at clearly recorded but different dates across cities.  
• We have a long balanced panel (22 years) and both pre- and post-treatment observations for most treated and comparison cities, satisfying the canonical DID data structure.  
• Event-study coefficients allow visual pre-trend tests and dynamic effect estimation.  
• RDD is infeasible (no sharp cutoff). IV not needed unless DiD assumptions fail.  

We will estimate:  
Pollution_cyt = β Treatment_cyt  +  γ_c + δ_t + X_cyt θ + ε_cyt  
and the same for infant mortality.  

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------  
A. Air programmes  
   Treatment variable:  
     1. SC_Action_cyt = 1 after a city’s Supreme Court Action Plan becomes binding.  
     2. Catalytic_cyt    = 1 after catalytic-converter mandate applies to the city.  
   Control group: cities not yet treated in a given year (including never-treated).  
   Timing: Delhi 1996, 16 additional cities, 1997-2003; catalytic: 4 metros 1995, 45 cities 1998.  

B. Water programme  
   Treatment variable: RiverPlan_cyt = 1 once a city receives its first NRCP sewerage project.  
   Control: river cities not yet funded in that year.  
   Timing: project start year from NRCP files (1985-2007, staggered).  

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel trends: In absence of treatment, pollution / infant mortality in treated and control cities would have followed similar trajectories.  
   • Plausible? Somewhat. Rapid national growth and health investments were economy-wide; still, treated cities are initially more polluted, so trends could differ. We will test with pre-treatment event-study coefficients.  

A2. No time-varying, city-specific shocks correlated with treatment.  
   • We include city-specific linear trends and census-derived, time-varying covariates (income, literacy, industrial composition).  

A3. No spillovers: treatment in city A does not affect outcomes in city B that is used as control.  
   • Air pollution can travel, but the vast majority of monitors are >50 km apart; water pollution spillovers run downstream—robustness will drop downstream cities.  

A4. Stable composition / SUTVA: monitor network and population measurement do not change systematically with treatment.  
   • We will restrict to monitors that appear both before and after treatment and include monitor fixed effects in pollution regressions.  

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
--------------------------------------------------  
T1. Policy endogeneity (selective targeting of dirtiest or most vocal cities).  
   • Mitigation:  
        – Control for lagged pollution levels.  
        – City linear trends.  
        – Instrumental-variables robustness: instrument treatment with the interaction of (i) year-specific national mandates and (ii) a city’s ex-ante eligibility (e.g., being one of the 17 designated “critically polluted areas” in 1991), though not in main spec.  

T2. Differential data coverage / attrition of monitors.  
   • Mitigation: balanced-panel monitors; monitor FE; cluster‐robust SE at city.  

T3. Concurrent national health programmes (e.g., NRHM after 2005).  
   • Mitigation: year FE capture nation-wide shocks; additionally interact year FE with state to soak up state-level programmes.  

5. R CODE OUTLINE  
--------------------------------------------------  
```r
# ================================================================
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(did)          # Callaway–Sant’Anna event-study
# ================================================================

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------
poll <- fread("city_pollution_1986_2007.csv")     # PM, SO2, NO2, BOD, etc.
treat <- fread("city_treatment_dates.csv")        # SC, Catalytic, NRCP dates
infant <- fread("city_infant_mortality.csv")      # IMR per 1,000 births
controls <- fread("city_covariates.csv")          # GDPpc, literacy, etc.

# 2. Merge & construct variables ---------------------------------
dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y,
                       by = c("city_id","year"), all = TRUE),
             list(poll, infant, controls))

# treatment dummies
dt[, SC_action := as.integer(year >= SC_start)]
dt[, Catalytic  := as.integer(year >= Cat_start)]
dt[, RiverPlan  := as.integer(year >= NRCP_start)]

# combine two air policies (main air treatment)
dt[, AirTreat := pmax(SC_action, Catalytic, na.rm = TRUE)]

# event-time for SC action
dt[, rel_time := year - SC_start]        # negative before treated

# 3. Main DID regression ------------------------------------------
est_air <- feols(log(PM10) ~ AirTreat + i(year) | city_id + year,
                 data = dt, cluster = "city_id")
summary(est_air)

est_health <- feols(IMR ~ AirTreat | city_id + year,
                    data = dt, cluster = "city_id")
summary(est_health)

# 4. Event-study (Callaway-Sant’Anna) -----------------------------
cs <- att_gt(yname = "PM10", tname = "year",
             idname = "city_id",
             gname = "SC_start",
             data = dt[!is.na(SC_start)])
es <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
summary(es)
plot(es)   # pre-trend check

# 5. Robustness: city-specific trends -----------------------------
est_air_trend <- feols(log(PM10) ~ AirTreat + i(year) | city_id + year +
                       city_id[year],          # city linear trends
                       data = dt, cluster="city_id")
summary(est_air_trend)
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------  
Prior: Supreme Court air regulations/catalytic converters decrease PM10 by roughly 10-20 μg/m³ (≈ 10–15 % relative to mean of 150 μg/m³). Infant mortality falls by 1–2 deaths per 1,000 live births (baseline urban IMR ≈ 40/1,000). River Conservation Plan likely shows little average effect because of weak enforcement and incomplete sewage links.  

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  
--------------------------------------------------  
C1. No differential pre-trends ………………… 0.7  
C2. No spillovers between units ……………… 0.6  
C3. No composition changes / SUTVA ……… 0.8  
C4. Treatment timing correctly measured …… 0.9  
C5. Common shocks adequately controlled ….. 0.8  

(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable; overall ≈ 3.8/5)
